translations.text: After Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian who came from the land of the Kittim, had struck down and killed Darius, king of the Persians and Medes, he became king in his place. He had first become king in Greece.
He fought great battles, captured many fortresses, and killed the kings of the earth.
He went to the ends of the earth and took plunder from many nations. The earth grew quiet and rested before him, and his heart became proud and arrogant.
He gathered a large, powerful army and ruled over peoples, nations, and rulers, who paid tribute to him.
After these things Alexander took to his bed and knew that he was dying.
He summoned his distinguished servants, who had grown up with him from his youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive.
Alexander reigned for twelve years and died.
His servants took possession, each of his own territory.
After his death they all put on crowns, and their sons succeeded them for many years. They multiplied evils on the earth.
From them came a sinful root, Antiochus Epiphanes, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage in Rome. He became king in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks.

In those days lawless men arose from Israel and persuaded many, saying to them, “Let us go and make a covenant with the nations around us, because ever since we separated from them, we have suffered many troubles.”
This proposal pleased them.
Some men from the people made plans and went to the king, and the king gave them permission to follow the customs of the nations.
The lawless men built an athletic arena in Jerusalem according to the customs of the nations.
They stretched out their foreskins, abandoned the holy covenant, mingled with the nations, and willingly committed evil deeds.
The kingdom was established and secured under Antiochus, and he wanted to rule over the land of Egypt as well, so that he might rule over both kingdoms.
Antiochus invaded Egypt with a large, powerful army, with chariots, elephants, cavalry, and great splendor.
He fought against Ptolemy, king of Egypt. Ptolemy was defeated before him, and they fled, and many fell dead.
They captured the fortified cities of Egypt and took the plunder of the land of Egypt.
After defeating Egypt, Antiochus returned in the one hundred and forty-third year. He also marched against Israel and came to Jerusalem with a powerful army.
He arrogantly entered the sanctuary and took the golden altar, the lampstand for the light, and all its equipment.

He also took the table for the bread of the Presence, the pitchers, the bowls, the golden vessels for sacrifices and offerings, the facings of the gateway, the wreaths, and all the gold decoration on the front of the temple. He stripped off all the workmanship.
He took the gold and silver and all the precious vessels, and he took the hidden treasures that he found.
Antiochus took everything and went to his own land. He carried out a great slaughter and spoke with great arrogance.
There was great mourning in Israel, in every place where they lived.
The leaders and elders groaned, as did the young men and young women, and the beauty of the women faded and changed.
Every bridegroom took up mourning, and the bride sitting in the bridal chamber mourned.
The earth shook on its pillars, and the whole house of Jacob clothed themselves in shame.
After two years King Antiochus sent the chief collector of tribute to the land of Judah. He came to Jerusalem with a large, powerful army.
He deceitfully spoke words of peace, and they believed him. Then he attacked the city without warning, struck it a great blow, and destroyed many people of Israel.
He took the city's plunder, burned it with fire, and demolished its houses and its surrounding wall.
He took their wives, children, and livestock captive, and they took possession of them.
They fortified the City of David with a great, strong wall and mighty towers, and it became a citadel for them.
They settled sinful people there, men who practiced wickedness, and they established themselves there.
They stored weapons and spears there, gathered all the plunder of Jerusalem, and put it there. It became a great trap.
It became an obstruction to the sanctuary, a stumbling block and an evil snare for Israel at all times.
They shed innocent blood around the sanctuary and defiled the sanctuary.
The inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them, and the city became a dwelling place for foreigners. She became a stranger to those born in her, and her children abandoned her.
The sanctuary was laid waste like a wilderness. Its festivals were turned into mourning, its Sabbaths into disgrace, and its honor into dishonor.
As great as its glory had been, so great was its disgrace, and its exaltation was turned into humiliation.
King Antiochus wrote to his entire kingdom that they should all become one people,
and that everyone should abandon their own law. All the nations agreed to act according to the king's command.
Many from Israel willingly adopted his worship, sacrificed to his idols, and profaned the Sabbath.
King Antiochus sent word through his messengers to Jerusalem and the villages of Judea that they should follow customs foreign to the land.
stop sacrifices, drink offerings, and offerings in the sanctuary, and profane the Sabbaths and festivals,
and defile the sanctuary and the holy things,
and build high places and temples for idols, set up idols, and slaughter pigs and unclean animals.
And to leave their sons uncircumcised, to defile themselves with every kind of impurity, and to profane themselves,
so that they would forget the law and change all the commandments.
Anyone who did not act according to the king's command was to die.
He wrote instructions like all these to his whole kingdom, appointed overseers over all the people, and commanded the towns of the Jews to offer sacrifices in every town.
Many of the people gathered around them—all those who had abandoned the law—and they committed many evil deeds in the land.
They drove Israel into hiding in all their places of refuge.

On the fifteenth day of the month of December, in the one hundred and forty-fifth year, they built the defilement of desolation upon the altar in the towns of Judea, and they built high places around it.
They offered sacrifices at the doors of the houses and in the streets.
They tore up the books of the Law that they found and burned them in the fire.
Wherever a book of the law was found, or anyone was found who delighted in the law, the king's decree sentenced that person to death.
In this way they violently oppressed Israel, all those who were found in the towns, month after month.
On the twenty-fifth day of the month, when they were offering sacrifices on that burnt offering which was on the altar,
they brought the women who had circumcised their sons and killed them according to the command.
While their children hung from their necks, they plundered their houses and killed those who had circumcised them.
Many in Israel took courage and stood firm, refusing to eat anything unclean.
They chose to die rather than defile themselves with food or break the holy covenant, and they died.
Great wrath came upon Israel.
In those days Mattathias son of John, son of Simon, a priest from the descendants of Jonadab, arose from Jerusalem and settled in Modein.
He had five sons: John, who was called Gaddi;
Simon, who was called Thassi;
Judas, who was called Maccabeus;
Eleazar, who was called Avaran; and Jonathan, who was called Apphus.
They saw the blasphemies being committed in Judea and Jerusalem.

He said, “Woe to me! Why was I born to see the ruin of my people and of the holy city? Foreigners have settled there, because it has been handed over to enemies, and its sanctuary into the hands of foreigners.”
Her temple was once like a glorious man.
“Now its glorious vessels have been carried away as plunder. Its children have been killed in its streets, and its young men by the enemy’s spear.”
What nation has not taken possession of her kingdom and taken some of her plunder?
All her splendor has been taken from her, and instead of being free she has become enslaved.
Look! Our sanctuary, our splendor, and our glory have become a ruin, and the nations have defiled them.
Why, then, should we go on living?”
Mattathias and his sons tore their clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourned deeply.
The king's officials, who were forcing people to apostatize, came to the town of Moraim [?] to make them offer sacrifices.
Many from Israel came to them, and Mattathias and those with him also gathered.
The king’s officials addressed Mattathias and said, “You are a leader, a great and honored man in this city, supported and upheld by sons and brothers.”

“Now, therefore, be the first to come forward and carry out the king’s command, as all the nations have done, along with the men of Judah who remain in Jerusalem. Then you and your sons will be among the king’s friends, and you and your sons will be honored with gold, silver, and various other gifts.”
Mattathias answered in a loud voice, “Even if all the nations under the king’s authority obey him, abandoning the worship of their ancestors and willingly accepting his commands,”
my sons, my brothers, and I will nevertheless live by the covenant of our ancestors.
Far be it from us to abandon the Lord’s law and his commandments!
“we will not obey the king’s word by breaking our covenant and abandoning our worship, or by turning aside from them to the right or to the left.”
When Mattathias had finished speaking these words, a Jewish man came forward in the sight of all the people to offer a sacrifice on the altar in Modein, as the king had commanded.
Mattathias saw him and burned with zeal. He trembled deep inside, and his righteous anger flared up. He ran and killed the man on the altar.
At the same time, he also killed the king’s officer who was forcing them to sacrifice, and he tore down the altar.
Mattathias showed zeal for the law, just as Phinehas had done against Zimri son of Salu.
Mattathias called out loudly in the city, “Let everyone who is zealous for the law and upholds the covenant follow me!”
He and his sons fled to the mountains, leaving behind everything they had in the city.
Then many who sought righteousness and justice went down into the wilderness to live there,
together with their wives, their children, and their livestock, because their troubles had become so great.
The king’s officials and the troops stationed in Jerusalem, in the City of David, were told that men who had defied the king’s command had gone down and were in hiding places in the wilderness.
Many soldiers rushed after them, caught up with them, and engaged them in battle on the Sabbath day.
They said to them, “You have gone far enough! Come out, do as the king commands, and live!”
They replied, “We will not come out, nor will we carry out the king’s order to violate and abolish the Sabbath day.”
The soldiers pressed the attack against them.
But they gave them no answer, nor did they throw a stone at them or block the entrances to their hiding places.
But they said, “Let us all die in our innocence. Heaven and earth bear witness for us that you are destroying us unjustly.”
They attacked them on the Sabbath day and killed them, their wives, their children, and their livestock—about a thousand people.
When Mattathias and his friends heard about it, they mourned deeply for them.
They said to one another, “If we all do as our brothers did and refuse to fight the Gentiles for our lives and our law, they will soon destroy us and wipe us off the earth.”
That day they took counsel and said, “If anyone comes to attack us on the Sabbath day, we will fight him. We will not all die as all our brothers died in their hiding places.”
Then a company of Hasideans from Israel joined Mattathias and his household. They were mighty warriors, all devoted to the law.
All those who were fleeing from these evils joined them and became a source of strength to them.
They raised an army and killed the wicked in their anger and those who broke the law in their fury. The rest fled to the Gentiles to escape.
Mattathias and his friends went around and tore down the altars.
They forcibly circumcised all the uncircumcised boys they found within the borders of Israel.
They pursued the arrogant, and their work prospered in their hands.
They rescued the law from the hands of the Gentiles and their kings, and did not allow the power of wickedness to rise.
When the time drew near for Mattathias to die, he said to his sons, “Now arrogance and punishment have grown strong; it is a time of destruction and fierce wrath.”
“Now, my sons, be zealous for the law and give your lives for the covenant of our ancestors.
which they did in their generations, and they received great glory and an everlasting name.
Was not Abraham found faithful when tested, and was it not counted to him as righteousness?
Joseph kept the commandment in the time of his distress and became lord of Egypt.
Our father Phinehas, because of the zeal he showed, received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.
Joshua, because he fulfilled the word, became a judge over Israel.
Caleb, because he testified in the assembly, received land as an inheritance.
David, through his mercy, inherited the throne of a kingdom that lasts forever and ever.
Elijah, because he was zealous for the law, was taken up to heaven.
Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, because they believed, were rescued from the fiery flame.
Daniel, because of his integrity, was rescued from the mouths of lions.
So consider this: in every generation, all who put their hope in him were neither brought low nor weakened.
Do not fear the words of a wicked man, for his glory will become dung and worms.
Today he is exalted, but tomorrow he is gone, because he has returned to his dust and his plans have perished.
But you, my sons, take courage and be strong in the law, for through it you will gain glory.
“Look, I know that your brother Simon is a man of counsel and understanding. Listen to him all your days, and he will be your leader and guide.”
“Judas Maccabeus has been a mighty warrior from his youth. He will be your leader and commander in battle, and he will fight battles against the Gentiles.”
Gather to yourselves all who observe the law, and avenge your people.”
Repay the Gentiles for what they have done, and pay attention to the commandments of the law.”
He blessed them and was gathered to his ancestors.
Mattathias died in the one hundred and forty-eighth year of the kingdom. His sons buried him in his ancestors’ tomb in Modein, and all Israel mourned deeply for him.
His son Judas Maccabeus rose up in his place.
All his brothers and all those who had followed his father helped him, and they fought Israel’s battles gladly and joyfully.
Judas increased and multiplied his people’s glory. He put on armor like a mighty warrior, equipped himself with his weapons of war, fought battles, and protected the camps with his spear.
In his deeds he was like a lion, like a young lion roaring for prey.
He diligently pursued the wicked, and he burned those who oppressed his people in the flames.
The wicked fled in terror before him, and all who practiced wickedness were shaken. Deliverance was brought about through his hands.
He embittered and distressed many kings, but brought joy and delight to Israel through his deeds. His memory will be a blessing forever.
He went through the towns of Judah, destroyed the wicked within them, and turned wrath away from Israel.
His fame reached the ends of the earth, and he gathered those who had been scattered.
Apollonius gathered the nations and a large force from Samaria to fight against Israel.
Judas learned of this and went out against them. He struck him down and killed him. Many of their men fell slain, and the rest fled.
They took their plunder. Judas also took Apollonius's sword and fought with it for the rest of his life.
Hieron, commander of the Syrian forces, heard that Judas had gathered around him a company of faithful men who went out to battle.
He said, “I will make a name for myself and gain glory throughout the kingdoms. I will fight Judas and those with him who despise the king’s command.”
He went up again, and a large and powerful army of wicked men went up with him to help him take revenge on the Israelites.
He reached the ascent of Beth-horon, and Judas went out to meet him with a few men.

When those with Judas saw the army coming against them, they said to Judas, “How can we, who are so few, fight against this whole powerful force? Besides, we are exhausted, for we have eaten nothing today.”
Judas said, “It is easy for many to be handed over to a few. Nothing prevents the one who lives in heaven from saving through many or through few.”
For victory in battle does not come through a large army; rather, strength is given from heaven.
“They are coming against us with a great force of wickedness and insolence, to destroy and wipe out us, our wives, and our children, and to take us captive.”
But we are fighting for our lives and our laws.
The Lord will crush them before us. Do not be afraid of them.”
When the Jew had finished speaking, he sprang forward and attacked them without warning. Hieron and his army fell before him.
Judas’s men pursued him down the descent of Beth-horon as far as the plain. About eight hundred of their men fell, and the rest fled to the land of the Philistines.
Fear of Judas and his brothers began to spread, and terror of them fell upon all the surrounding nations.
His fame reached the king, and all the nations were recounting Judas's deeds.
When Antiochus heard these reports, he became furious. He sent orders to gather all the forces of his kingdom, a large and powerful army.
He opened his treasury and gave his troops a year’s pay. He ordered them to be ready and prepared for anything.

He saw that the money in his treasury had dwindled and that the revenues from the land were small because of the division and devastation he had caused in the land by seeking to abolish their ancestral laws.
He was afraid that he might not have enough to give once or twice more, since he had been giving lavishly, more generously than the kings before him.
Antiochus was deeply troubled within himself and decided to go to Persia to collect the revenues of the land and gather a large amount of money.
He left Lysias, a distinguished man of royal descent, in charge of the king’s affairs from the Euphrates River to the border of Egypt.
and to bring up his son Antiochus until he returned.
He entrusted the elephants and half his army to him and gave him instructions about everything he wanted done, including what was to be done about the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem:
to send an army against them to wipe out and completely destroy Israel’s strength, to destroy those who remained in Jerusalem, and to erase their memory from the place.
and to settle foreigners throughout their territory and give them possession of their land.
The king took the remaining half of the army and set out from Antioch, the capital of his kingdom, in the year 147. He crossed the Euphrates River and traveled through the upper provinces.
Lysias chose Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, Nicanor, and Gorgias, capable men from among the king’s friends.
He sent with them forty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry to go to the land of Judea and devastate it, as the king had commanded.
Ptolemy and his men set out with their entire army and came and camped beside Emmaus, in the plain.

The merchants of the land heard about them, took large amounts of silver and gold, along with chains and shackles, and came to the camp to buy the Israelites as slaves. The Syrian forces and the Philistine people also joined them.

Judas and his brothers saw that their troubles were many and that an army had surrounded their territory. They also learned of the king’s orders concerning the people, that they were to be destroyed and wiped out.
They said to one another, “Let us restore our fallen people and fight for our people and our holy places.”
Their assembly gathered to prepare for battle, to pray, and to ask for mercy and compassion.

Jerusalem was a deserted ruin, with none of its children entering or leaving it. Its sanctuary was being trampled, and foreigners were living in its citadel. It had become a lodging place for the nations. Joy had been taken away from Jacob, and harps and lyres had disappeared from it.
They gathered and went to Mizpah, opposite Jerusalem, because Mizpah had been a place of prayer for Israel since ancient times.
They fasted that day, clothed themselves in sackcloth, put dust on their heads, and tore their clothes.
They unrolled the scroll of the Law and complained before the Holy One about the nations who were forcing them to live as they did.
They brought the priestly garments, the firstfruits, and the tithes, and presented the Nazirites who had completed the days of their Nazirite vows.
They cried out to the one who dwells in heaven and said, “What shall we do with these, or where shall we take them?
Look, your sanctuary is being trampled and defiled, and your priests are in mourning and humiliation.
Look, the nations have gathered against us to wipe us out. You know what they are plotting against us.
How can we stand against them unless you help us?”
They sounded the horns and cried out with a loud voice.
After this, Judas appointed leaders over the people: commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, and commanders of fifty.
He told those who had built houses, those who were engaged to women, those who had planted vineyards, and those who were afraid that each should return home, as the Law said.
The army set out and camped south of Emmaus.
Judas said, “Take courage and be brave. Be ready in the morning to fight these nations who have gathered against us to destroy us and our sanctuary.”
For it is better for us to die in battle than to witness the ruin of our people and our sanctuary.
Whatever the will of the one who dwells in heaven may be, so he will act.”
Gorgias took with him five thousand infantry and a thousand picked cavalry, and his army set out by night.
Their purpose was to attack Judas’s camp by night and kill them by surprise. Those who lived in the citadel served as their guides.
Judas heard about this, and he and the warriors with him set out to attack the king’s army at Emmaus,
while its forces were scattered away from its camp.
Gorgias came to Judas’s camp but found no one. He searched for them in the mountains, for he said, “These men have fled from us.”
When morning came, Judas appeared in the plain with three thousand infantry. They had nothing with them except spears and shields, as they wanted.
They saw the army of the nations, a strong army equipped with weapons, with cavalry surrounding it, all trained for battle.
Judas said to the men with him, “Do not be afraid of their numbers or alarmed by their preparations.
Remember how our ancestors were delivered at the Red Sea when Pharaoh pursued them with a great army.
“Now let us cry out to the one who dwells in heaven, so that he may have mercy on us and the Lord may remember the covenant with our ancestors and crush this army before us today.”
And all the nations will know that there is someone who redeems and rescues Israel.
The Philistines looked up and saw them coming to meet them.
They came out of their camps for battle, and Judas’s men sounded the horns.
They attacked them, and the nations were defeated and fled to the plain.
The rest who remained fell by the sword. They pursued them as far as Gezer, the plain of Edom, Gaza, and Jamnia. About three thousand of their men fell.
Judas and his army returned from pursuing them.
He said to the people, “Do not be eager for plunder, because there is still a battle ahead of us.
“Gorgias and his army are in the mountains, and they are near us. Instead, stand now against our enemies and fight them. Afterward you can take the plunder openly.”
While Judas was saying this, some of the men with Gorgias looked out from the mountain.
They saw that it had been defeated and that Judas’s men were burning their camps, for the visible smoke revealed what had happened.
When they saw these things, they were very afraid, especially when they also saw Judas’s army in the plain, ready for battle.
They all fled to the land of the Philistines.
Judas returned to plunder the camp and took much gold and silver, precious stones of jacinth, purple from the sea, and great wealth.
They returned, praising and giving thanks to the Lord in heaven, for he is good and his mercy lasts forever.
There was deliverance for Israel that day.
The survivors among the Philistines came and told Lysias what had happened.
When he heard, he lost heart and was deeply distressed, because what he had wanted had not happened to Israel, and he had not carried out the king’s command.
At the end of the year, Lysias gathered sixty thousand picked men and five thousand cavalry to fight against Israel.
They came to Edom and camped at Beth-zur, and Judas met them with ten thousand men.

He saw the army of their enemies, a strong army, and prayed, saying, “Blessed are you, the Savior of Israel, who crushed the mighty warrior’s confidence by the hand of your servant David. You delivered the army of the Philistines into the hands of Jonathan son of Saul and his armor-bearer. Now also deliver this army into the hands of your people Israel.”
Let them be put to shame over their army and their cavalry.
Cast fear upon them, shatter the strength of their army, and let them tremble at their downfall.
Strike them down with the spears of those who love you, and let all who know your name praise you with songs of praise.”
They fought one another, and about five thousand men from Lysias’s army fell, and they were crushed before them.

When Lysias saw that his army had been defeated, that Judas’s army had grown strong, and that they were courageously prepared to die or live, he departed from there and went to Antioch. He gathered a large army, made preparations, and planned to march against Judea again.
Judas and his brothers said, “Look, our enemies have been crushed. Let us go up, cleanse the sanctuary, and rededicate it.”
The whole army assembled, and they went up to Mount Zion.
They saw the sanctuary laid waste, the altar ruined, and the gates burned. Trees had sprung up in the courtyards as in a forest or on one of the mountains, and all the [?] had been torn down.
They tore their clothes, mourned deeply, and put dust on their heads.
They fell facedown on the ground, sounded the signal horns, and cried out to the one who dwells in heaven.
Then Judas gave orders and appointed men to engage and fight those who lived in the fortresses until he had cleansed the sanctuary.
He chose priests who were without blemish and delighted in the Law.
He cleansed the sanctuary, took away the defiled stones, and put them in an unclean place.
They discussed what they should do with the altar of sacrifice, which had been defiled.
They decided it would be best to dismantle it, lest it remain a lasting reproach to them because the nations had defiled it. So they dismantled the altar.
They placed its stones in a known place beside the chambers of the temple, until a prophet should come and say what should be done with them.
They took whole stones, as prescribed in the Law, and rebuilt the altar as it had been before.
They rebuilt the sanctuary and consecrated the entire interior of the temple and the courtyards.
They made new sacred vessels and brought the lampstand, the incense altar, and the table into the temple.
They offered sacrifices on the altar and lit the lamps on the lampstand, and they shone in the temple.
They placed bread on the table, hung the doors, and completed all their work.
They rose early in the morning on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, which is December, in the one hundred and forty-eighth year of the kingdom.
They offered sacrifices according to the law on the new altar of burnt offerings that they had made.
On the very same day and at the same season when the nations had defiled it, it was rededicated with songs, harps, and lyres.
All the people fell facedown, worshiped, and blessed the one who dwells in heaven, who had established and prepared their way.
They celebrated the dedication of the altar for eight days, offering sacrifices with gladness and sacrificing offerings of deliverance and praise.
They decorated the front of the temple with gold crowns and shields, and restored the gates and all the ornamental furnishings.
There was great rejoicing and abundant joy among the people, and the disgrace brought by the nations was removed.

Judas, his brothers, and the whole assembly of Israel decreed that the days of the dedication of the altar should be observed at their appointed time every year for eight days, beginning on the twenty-fifth of December, with joy and gladness.
At that time they fortified Mount Zion all around with high walls and strong towers, so that the nations might never again come and trample it as they had done before.
They stationed troops there to guard it, and he strengthened Beth-zur so that the people would have a fortress facing Edom.
When the surrounding nations heard that the altar had been rebuilt and the sanctuary restored as it had been before, they became very angry.
They planned to go up and wipe out the descendants of Jacob who lived among them, and they began killing and spreading destruction among the people.
Judas fought against the descendants of Esau in Edom, at Akrabattene, because they were besieging Israel. He inflicted a great defeat on them, scattered them, and took their plunder.
He remembered the wicked deeds of the descendants of Baean, who had been a trap and a stumbling block to the people, lying in ambush for them along the roads.
He shut them up in their towers, attacked them, and devoted them to destruction. He burned their towers with everything in them.
Judas crossed over against the Ammonites and found a strong people and a powerful force, with Timothy as their commander.
He fought great battles against them, and they were crushed before him, and he struck them down.
He captured Jazer and its surrounding towns, and Judas returned to Edom.
The nations in Gilead gathered against the Israelites who lived within their borders, intending to wipe them out, and the Israelites fled to the fortress of Ramath.
They sent letters to Judas and his brothers, saying, “The nations around us have gathered against us to wipe us out.
Now they are preparing to come and capture this fortress in which we are holding out, and Timothy is their commander.
So come now and rescue us from their hands, because many of our people have fallen."
All our brothers who were in Tob have died. Their wives, children, and all their wealth have been taken captive, and about a thousand men perished there.”
While these letters were being read, other messengers arrived from Galilee, tearing their clothes and reporting similar things.
They said that foreign nations from Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon, and all Galilee had gathered against them: “They intend to wipe us out and destroy us completely.”
When Judas and all the people heard these reports, they gathered in a great assembly to discuss what they should do for their brothers who were in distress and being oppressed by those nations.
Judas said to his brother Simon, “Gather men and go rescue your brothers in Galilee. My brother Jonathan and I will go to Gilead.”
He left Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah, leaders of the people, with the rest of the army in Judea to keep guard.
He commanded them, saying, “See that you take care of this people, and do not engage in battle with the nations until we return.”
Three thousand men were assigned to Simon to go with him to Galilee, and eight thousand to Judas to go to Gilead.
Simon went to Galilee and fought great battles against the Gentiles, and the Gentiles were defeated before him.
He pursued them as far as Ptolemais. About three thousand of the Gentiles fell, and his men took their spoils.
Simon took those who were in Galilee and Arbatta, together with their wives, their children, and all their possessions, and brought them to Judea with great joy.
Judas Maccabeus and his brother Jonathan crossed the Jordan and traveled for three days through the wilderness.
The Nabateans met them, received them peacefully, and told them everything that had happened to their fellow Israelites in Gilead.
They said that many of them were shut up in Bozrah, Bosor, Alema, Casphor, Makar, and Carnaim, all of them large and fortified cities.
Others were shut up in the remaining cities of Gilead, and their enemies were preparing to attack the fortresses the next day, overthrow them, and destroy everyone in a single day.
Judas and his whole army turned toward Bozrah by the wilderness road. He suddenly attacked the city, and they killed every male in it with the sword. He took all their spoils and burned the city.
Judas set out from there at night, and they traveled as far as the fortress.
When morning came, they looked up and saw an immense, countless crowd carrying ladders and ropes and advancing to capture the fortress.
Judas saw that the battle was fierce, that the city's outcry rose to heaven, and that there was the sound of horns and a great uproar.
Judas said to the soldiers, “Fight today for your brothers!”
Judas advanced in three divisions from behind them. They sounded the horns and cried out in prayer.
Timothy's army recognized that it was Maccabeus, and they fled before him. He inflicted a crushing defeat on them, and about eight thousand of their men fell that day.
Judas turned aside to Alema and fought against it. They killed every male in it, took its spoils, and burned it.
From there Judas set out and captured Casphor, Makar, Bosora, and the remaining cities of Gilead.
After these events, Timothy gathered another army and camped near Raphon, on the other side of the river.
Judas sent men to scout his camp. They returned and told him, “All the Gentiles around us have gathered against you, a large and powerful army.
They have also hired Arabs to help them. They are camped on the other side of the river and are ready to come against you in battle.” So Judas went to meet them.

Timothy said to the commanders of his army, “When Judas and his army approach the riverbank, if he crosses over to us first, we will not be able to stand against him, because our strength will be utterly exhausted.”
But if he is afraid and camps on the other side of the river, we will cross over to him, and his army will be defeated.”
When Judas reached the river, he stationed the people's scribes beside it and commanded them, “Do not allow anyone at all to make camp. Everyone must come to battle.”
He crossed over against them first, with all the people following him. The Gentiles were defeated before him, threw down their weapons, and fled to the temple of idols in Carnaim.
Judas's men captured the city and burned the temple of idols with everything in it. Carnaim was defeated and could no longer stand against Judas.

Judas gathered all the Israelites in Gilead, from the least to the greatest, together with their wives, their children, and all their possessions—a large and mighty company—to go to the land of Judea.
He came as far as Ephron, a large and very strongly fortified city situated on the road. There was no way around it, either to the right or to the left; they had to pass through it.
The inhabitants of the town shut them out and blocked the gates with stones.

Judas sent them a peaceful message, saying, “Let me pass through your land and go to our own land. No one will harm you; we will simply pass through on foot.” But they refused to open the gates for them.
Judas ordered a proclamation to be made throughout the camp that everyone should encamp where he was.
The soldiers encamped and fought against the city all that day and all that night, and the city was delivered into his hands.
He killed every male in it with the sword. They demolished it, took its spoils, and passed through the city over the bodies of the slain.
They crossed the Jordan into the great plain opposite Beth-shan.
Judas gathered up those who were straggling behind and encouraged the people all along the way until they reached the land of Judea.
They went up to Mount Zion with delight and joy and offered sacrifices and burnt offerings, because not even one of them had fallen, and they returned in peace.
In those days Judas and his brother Jonathan were in the land of Gilead, and his brother Simon was in Galilee, opposite Ptolemais.
Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah, the commanders of the armies, heard about Judas's bravery, victories, and battles.
They said, “Let us also make a name for ourselves. Let us go and fight against the nations around us.”
They gave orders to the army with them and went to Jamnia.
Gorgias and the men with him came out of the city to meet them in battle.
Joseph and Azariah were defeated, and their enemies pursued them as far as the border of Edom. About two thousand men of the people of Israel fell that day.
There was a great defeat in Israel because they had not obeyed Judas and his brothers, since they too wanted to win a name and victory for themselves.
But they were not descendants of those men through whom God had brought deliverance to Israel.
Judas and his brothers were greatly honored in the sight of all Israel, among all the nations, and wherever their fame was heard.
People would gather and come to praise them.

Judas and his brothers went out and fought against the descendants of Esau in the southern land. They attacked Hebron and its surrounding towns, demolished its fortifications, and burned its towers all around. Then Judas set out from there to go to the land of the Philistines.
He passed through Samaria.
On that day priests fell in battle because they wanted to win glory for themselves and went out to battle without taking counsel.
Judas turned toward Azotus in the land of the Philistines. They demolished their high places, burned their carved idols in the fire, and plundered the cities. Then he returned to the land of Judah.
King Antiochus was traveling through the upper regions when he heard that in Persia there was a city, Elam, renowned for its wealth in gold and silver.

The temple of its idols was very rich. There were gold helmets, breastplates, and weapons there, which Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian king who was the first king of the Greeks, had left there.
He came and tried to capture the city and plunder it, but he could not, because the inhabitants of the city had learned of the matter.
They rose against him in battle, and he fled and departed from there in great distress to return to Babylon.
People came and told Antiochus in Persia that his armies that had gone to Judah had been defeated.

And how Lysias had first gone with a large army and had been defeated by them, and how Judas's men had grown strong in weapons, military power, and the great amount of plunder they had taken from the armies they had defeated.
They had demolished the abomination that had been built on the altar in Jerusalem, and had surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as before, and also Beth-zur, their city.
When the king heard these reports, he was astonished and deeply shaken. He took to his bed and became ill with grief because things had not turned out as he had expected.
He remained there for many days, because his distress kept returning, and Antiochus thought that he was dying.
He called all his friends and said to them, "Sleep has left my eyes, and my heart has melted within me from so much worry.
I said to myself, 'What distress I have come to, and what a great storm I am caught in! Yet I was kind and loved during my reign.'
But now I remember the evils I committed in Jerusalem: I took the gold and silver vessels that were in it, and I sent orders to destroy the inhabitants of Judah for no reason.
I know that all these troubles have come upon me because of these things. Now I am dying of great grief in a foreign land."
Antiochus summoned Philip, one of his friends, and appointed him over his whole kingdom.
He gave him his crown, robe, and ring to bring to his son Antiochus, and charged him to bring the boy up to be king.
King Antiochus died there in the year 149.
Lysias learned that the king had died, and he installed the king's son Antiochus in his place as king. He had brought him up from childhood, and he named him Eupator.
Those living in the citadel were hemming Israel in on every side of the sanctuary. They wanted to do every kind of harm and were giving help to the nations.
Judas decided to drive them out and gathered all the people to besiege them.
They gathered together and laid siege to them in the year one hundred and fifty. They built siege towers and engines to fight against them.
Some of them escaped from the place where they were confined, and wicked men from Israel joined them.
They went to the king and said to him, “How long will you fail to carry out justice and avenge our brothers?”
We are willing to serve your father, to follow all his commands, and to carry out all his wishes.
And now our fellow countrymen are occupying the citadel because of this. We have become like foreigners to them, and they kill any of us they find, and our inheritance is being plundered by them.
They have stretched out their hands not only against us, but also against all their territories.
And now they are besieging the citadel in Jerusalem to capture it, and they have strengthened the sanctuary and Beth-zur.
Unless you move against them quickly, they will do greater and worse things than these, and you will not be able to withstand their strength.
The king became angry when he heard these things, and he gathered all his friends, the commanders of his army, and those assigned to the chariots.
And from other kingdoms and from many islands, troops hired by him came to him.
His army numbered one hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants trained for battle.
They came into Edom, besieged Beth-zur, and fought for many days. They made siege engines, but the defenders came out, burned them with fire, and fought bravely.
Judas departed from the citadel and encamped beside Beth-zechariah, opposite the king’s camp.
The king rose early in the morning and led his army swiftly along the road to Beth-zechariah. The troops prepared for battle and sounded the horns.
They showed the elephants the juice of grapes and mulberries and prepared them for battle.

They divided them into units and assigned to each elephant a thousand men wearing iron armor and bronze helmets on their heads. Five hundred cavalry were attached to each elephant, men who had been chosen
beforehand. Wherever one of the elephants went, these men went there too, and they did not move away from it.
Above them were strong wooden towers covering each elephant, secured with mechanical devices. On each one were thirty fighting men who fought from it, along with its driver.
They stationed the remaining cavalry on either side of the army, fighting and displaying their weapons among the divisions.
When the sun rose and shone on the gold and bronze shields, the mountains gleamed and flashed with their light like flaming torches.
Part of his army formed ranks and took its position on the high mountains, and part on the lower hills. They advanced confidently in their ranks.
Everyone who heard the sound of their army, the marching of their multitude, and the clashing of their weapons trembled, for it was a great and very powerful army.
Judas and his army advanced into battle, and six hundred men from the king’s army fell.
Eleazar, who was called Avaran, saw one of the elephants equipped with royal armor. It stood out above all the other elephants, and it appeared that the king was on it.
He gave his life to save his people and to make an everlasting name for himself.
He ran at it with strength and courage through the armies and divisions, striking down men to his right and left, and they fled before him in every direction.
He went underneath the elephant, struck it in the belly with his sword, and killed it. It fell to the ground on top of him, and he died there.
Judas saw the strength of the kingdom and the readiness of its army, and he withdrew from them.
Some of the king’s army went up against them to Jerusalem, and the king encamped in Judea and on Mount Zion.
He made peace with those in Beth-zur, and they left the city because they had no provisions to remain shut up inside it, since it was a sabbath year for the land.
The king captured Beth-zur and stationed a garrison there to guard it.
He besieged the sanctuary and fought against it for many days. They set up towers and siege engines there to fight against them and to launch arrows, stones, and fire with catapults.
They too made siege engines to counter their siege engines, and they fought for many days.
There were no provisions in the sanctuary because it was the seventh year, and those who had escaped from among the nations had eaten the remainder of their food supplies.
Only a few people remained in the temple, because the famine had become severe among them, and they had scattered, each to his own place.
Lysias heard that Philip, whom Antiochus had appointed while he was still alive to raise his son and make him king,
had returned from Persia and Media with the entire army that had gone with the king, and that he wanted to take control of the affairs of the kingdom.

He was in a hurry to leave, and Lysias said to the king, the army commanders, and the leaders of the people, “We are wearing ourselves out here, and we have little food. This place we are besieging is very strongly fortified, and the affairs of the kingdom are our responsibility.
Now let us offer these men our right hand and make peace with them and with all their people.
Let us guarantee them the right to live according to their laws as they did before, for it was because we abolished their laws that they became angry and enraged and did all these things.”
The proposal pleased the king and his officials, and he sent word to them to make peace with them, and they accepted it.
The king and his leaders swore an oath to them, and on these terms they came out of their fortress.
The king entered Mount Zion and saw how strongly fortified the place was. He broke the oaths he had sworn and ordered its surrounding wall to be demolished.
He left there and hurried back to Antioch. He found that Philip had seized the city and taken control of it, so he fought against him and took the city from him by force.
In the year one hundred and fifty-one, Demetrius son of Seleucus left Rome and came with a few men to the coastal cities, where he became king.
As he was entering the royal palace of his ancestors, the troops arrested Antiochus and Lysias to bring them to him.
When the matter became known to him, he said, “Do not let me see their faces.”
So the soldiers killed them, and Demetrius sat on the throne of his kingdom.
All the lawless and wicked men of Israel came to him. Their leader was Alcimus, who wanted to become high priest.
They slandered the people before the king and said, “Judas and his brothers have killed your friends and driven us out of our land.
Now send a man you trust, and let him go and see all the destruction they have brought upon us and upon the king’s land, and how to punish them and all their supporters.”
The king chose his friend Bacchides, who governed the region beyond the River and was an important and trusted man in his kingdom.
He sent him and the wicked Alcimus, whom he appointed to the priesthood, and commanded him to take vengeance on the Israelites.
They set out and came to the land of Judah with a large army. They deceitfully sent messengers to Judas and his brothers with words of peace.
They examined and considered their words, for they saw that they had come against them with a large army.
A group of scribes gathered before Alcimus and Bacchides to make inquiries and seek justice.
The worshipers among the Israelites were the first, and they sought peace from them.
For they said, “A priest descended from Aaron has come with the army, and they will not harm us.”
He spoke peaceful words to them and swore an oath to them, saying, “We will neither seek nor plan harm against you or your friends.”
They believed him, but he seized sixty of their men and killed them in a single day, according to the word spoken by the prophet.
The flesh of your faithful ones, and their blood they poured out around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.
Fear of them fell upon all the people, for they said, “There is neither truth nor justice in them, for they have violated the agreement, the oaths, and the covenant they made.”
Bacchides left Jerusalem, and they camped at Bezeth. He sent men and arrested some of those who had rebelled against him, as well as some of the people, and slaughtered them at the great cistern.
He handed the country over to Alcimus and left troops with him to help him. Then Bacchides went to the king.
Alcimus, meanwhile, was fighting for the high priesthood.
All those who were stirring up trouble among their own people gathered around him. He took control of the land of Judah and inflicted a great blow on Israel.
Judas saw all the evil that Alcimus and those with him had done to the Israelites, worse than what the Gentiles had done.
He went throughout all the surrounding territory of Judah and carried out judgment on the men who had rebelled and had been sent to travel through the land.
When Alcimus saw that Judas and those with him had grown strong, and realized that he could not stand against them, he returned to the king and slandered them with many malicious accusations.
King Demetrius sent Nicanor, one of his distinguished officials, who was full of hatred and hostility toward Israel, and commanded him to wipe out and destroy the people.
Nicanor came to Jerusalem with a large army and deceitfully sent words of peace to Judas and his brothers, saying to them:
“Let there be no conflict between me and you. I will come with a few men and meet you in peace.”
They came to Judas and greeted one another, but the troops were ready to seize Judas.
Judas learned that they had come to him deceitfully, so he withdrew from Nicanor and would no longer agree to see him.
Nicanor realized that his plan had been discovered, and he went out to meet Judas in battle near Caphar-salama.
About five hundred of Nicanor's men fell, and they fled to the City of David.

After these events, Nicanor went up to Mount Zion. The priests came out of the sanctuary, along with some of the elders of the people, to greet him and show him the burnt offerings and sacrifices being offered on behalf of the king.
He mocked and ridiculed them, treated them with contempt, and spoke arrogantly.
He swore in anger and said, “Unless Judas and his army are handed over to me now, I will burn down this house when I return safely.” Then he left in great anger.
The priests went in and stood before the altar and the sanctuary, weeping and saying,
You, Lord, chose this house for yourself, so that your name would be called upon it and it would be a house of prayer and supplication for your people.
Take vengeance on this man and his army, and let them fall by the spear. Remember their blasphemy, and give them no strength or endurance.
Nicanor left Jerusalem and camped at Beth-horon, where the Syrian army joined him.
Judas camped at Adasa with three thousand men. Judas prayed and said,
Lord, you are the one whose angel went out and destroyed a hundred and eighty-five thousand soldiers when the forces of the king of Assyria blasphemed against you.
In the same way, crush and shatter this army before us today. Let the rest know that they spoke wickedly against your sanctuary, and judge them according to their wickedness.
The armies began to fight on the thirteenth of the month of Adar. Nicanor’s army was defeated, and he was the first to fall in battle.
When Nicanor’s army saw that he had fallen, they threw down their weapons and fled.
Judas and his men pursued them for a day’s journey, from Adasa until they reached Gazara, sounding signals on horns behind them.
People came out from all the villages of Judea, gathered together, and drove them back against one another, until they all fell by the edge of the sword. Not even one of them remained.
They took their plunder and captives, and they took Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had raised arrogantly. They brought them to Jerusalem and hung them up.
The people rejoiced greatly, and they celebrated that day with feasting and joy.
They decreed that they would celebrate it every year on the thirteenth of the month of Adar.
The land of Judah was quiet for a few days.
Judas heard the reports about the Romans: that they were powerful in battle, welcomed all who joined them, and established friendship with everyone who approached them.
People told him about their bravery and the wars they had fought against the Galatians, how they had prevailed over them and made them pay tribute.
They also told him everything they had done in the land of Spain, and how they had seized the gold and silver mines there.

They had captured their kings and, through their perseverance, every place, though the region was very far from them. They had also crushed the kings who came against them from the ends of the earth, inflicting a great defeat on them, while the rest paid them tribute every year.
They had also humbled Philip, the kings of the Hittites, and those who rose against them, crushing them in battle and prevailing over them.
As for Antiochus, the great king of Asia, who had gone to war against them with a hundred and twenty elephants, cavalry, chariots, and a large and powerful force, they crushed his entire army.
They captured him alive, and he agreed that he and the kings who succeeded him would pay them a large tribute every year and give hostages and payments.
They took from him the lands of India, Media, and Lydia, choice lands among his territories, and gave them to King Eumenes.
Again, when those from Greece wanted to come to wipe them out and destroy them,

When the matter became known to them, they sent one of their generals against them. He fought them, and many of them were killed. They took their wives and children captive, plundered them, seized their land and gained control over it, demolished their fortresses, and subjected them to this day.
They also destroyed the remaining kingdoms and islands—in short, all who opposed them—plundering them, taking captives, and reducing them to slavery.

But they maintained friendship with their friends and with those who relied on them. They gained power and prevailed over kings both far and near, and everyone who heard reports about them trembled before them.
Anyone they wished to help and make king became king, and anyone they wished to humble they humbled. They rose to great prominence and power.
Yet despite all this, not one of them put on a crown or clothed himself in purple to exalt himself through these things.
They established a senate house for themselves, and every day three hundred and twenty men, members of the council, deliberated together, considering how to care for and govern the people.

They entrusted the leadership to one man for a year, and he commanded and exercised authority over their whole land. They all obeyed that one man, and there was neither envy nor jealousy among them. Judas chose Eupolemus son of John, son of Accos, and Jason son of Eleazar.
He sent them to Rome to establish friendship and mutual assistance with them.
so that they might remove the yoke from them, because the kingdom of the Greeks was reducing Israel to slavery.
Eupolemus and his companions went to Rome. The journey was very long. They entered the Romans’ senate house and addressed them, saying:
“Judas Maccabeus, his brothers, and the Jewish people have sent us to you to establish an alliance and friendship with you, and to have you enroll us as your friends and allies.”
The proposal pleased them.
This is the copy of the letter that they inscribed on a bronze tablet and sent to Jerusalem to remain with them as a memorial of friendship, alliance, and peace.
May all go well for the Romans and the Jewish people at sea and on land forever, and may spear and enemy remain far from them.
But if war should first arise against the Romans, or against any of their allies, or anywhere under their authority,
the Jewish people shall come wholeheartedly to their aid, as circumstances require.

they shall give no relief to the enemies fighting against them, and shall withhold grain, weapons, money, and ships from them, as the Romans have decided. They shall fulfill their obligations without receiving anything from them.
But if war should first befall the Jewish people, the Romans shall fight and help them wholeheartedly, as the circumstances require.

No grain, weapons, money, or ships shall be given to those fighting and waging war against them, as the Romans have decided. They shall fulfill their obligations without receiving anything from them, and without deceit.
On these terms the Romans made an agreement with the Jewish assembly.
But if, after these terms, they wish to remove or add anything, they may do whatever seems good to them. Whatever they remove or add shall be binding on them.
Concerning the wrongs that King Demetrius has done to you, we have written and sent him this message: “Why have you made your yoke heavy and harsh upon our friends and allies, the Jews?”
If they complain about you again, we will obtain redress and justice for them, and wage war against you by sea and by land.”
Demetrius heard that Nicanor and his army had fallen in battle, and he again sent Bacchides and Alcimus to the land of Judah, for the second time, with the army's right wing accompanying them.
Bacchides and his men went by the road through Gilead and camped against Mesaloth in Arbela. They captured it and burned many people there.
In the first month of the year 152, they camped against Jerusalem.
Then they moved on and went to Berezeth with twenty thousand infantry and two thousand cavalry.
Judas was camped at Elasa, with three thousand chosen men.
They saw that their enemies' army was very strong and became terribly afraid. Many deserted the camp, and only eight hundred men remained.
Judas saw that his army had scattered and that battle was pressing upon him. He was crushed in spirit and lost heart, because he had no time to gather them.
He said to those who remained with him, “Get up, and let us advance against our enemies. Perhaps we can fight them.”
They turned away from him and said to him, “We cannot do it. Instead, let us save our lives now, and return with our brothers and fight them, because we are few.”
Judas said, “Far be it from me to do this and flee before them! If our time has come, let us die bravely for our brothers and leave no stain on our honor.”

The army moved out from the camp and took its position for battle. The cavalry divided into two divisions, and the archers and slingers went ahead of the army, with all the mighty warriors and fighting men.
Bacchides was on the right wing. The divisions on both sides advanced and sounded their horns, and Judas and his men also sounded their horns.
The earth shook with the noise of the armies, and they fought from morning until evening.
Judas saw that Bacchides and the strongest part of the army were on the right side, and his companions committed themselves wholeheartedly.
The right wing was broken and crushed before them, and he pursued them as far as Mount Azotus.
When those on the left side saw that the right side had been defeated, they turned to follow Judas and those with him, coming up behind them.
They intensified the battle, and men fell on both sides.
Judas too fell, and those who remained fled.
Jonathan and Simon took their brother Judas and buried him in the tomb of his ancestors at Modein.
All Israel wept and performed mourning dances for Judas. They mourned deeply for him for many days and said:
“How the mighty warrior has fallen, the savior of Israel!”
The rest of Judas's deeds, his battles, his victories, his bravery, and his mighty acts were not written down, for they were very numerous.
After Judas's death, lawless men emerged and appeared throughout the territory of the Israelites, and all the wicked and those who violated the law showed themselves.
In those days there was a great famine, and the land too was devastated along with them.
Bacchides chose wicked men and appointed them as masters and rulers over the land.
They searched for Judas's friends and tracked them down, bringing them to Bacchides, who mocked and tortured them.
There was great distress in Israel, unlike anything that had happened since a prophet was last seen among them.
All Judas’s friends gathered and said to Jonathan:
“Since the day your brother Judas died, there has been no man like him to go out against our enemies, against Bacchides, and against all those among our own people who fight against us and hate us.”
Now, today, we choose you to be our chief and leader and to fight our battles.”
At that time Jonathan agreed to become their leader, and he took the place of his brother Judas.
Bacchides learned of this and wanted to kill him.
Jonathan, his brother Simon, and everyone with him learned of this, and they fled to the wilderness of Tekoa and camped by the water at the cistern of Asphar.
Bacchides learned of this on the Sabbath day, and he and his entire army came to the banks of the Jordan.
Jonathan sent his brother John to lead the people, and asked his friends the Nabateans to let him leave all their baggage with them.
The sons of Jambri came out from Medeba, seized John and everything he had with him, and carried them away.

After these events, Jonathan and his brother Simon were told that the sons of Jambri were holding a great wedding feast and were bringing a bride from Nabath, the daughter of one of the leading nobles of Canaan, with great celebration and a large crowd.
Jonathan remembered his brother John, and they went up and hid on the mountainside.
They looked up and saw a large, noisy crowd, and the bridegroom and his friends. His friends and brothers had come out to meet him with lyres, harps, and many weapons.
Jonathan's men rose against them from their ambush and killed them. Many fell dead, and the rest fled to the mountain. They took all their plunder.
The wedding feast turned into mourning, and the sound of their music into wailing.
They avenged their brother’s blood and returned to the other side of the Jordan.
Bacchides heard that Jonathan had returned, and he came to the banks of the Jordan on the Sabbath day with a large army.
Jonathan said to those with him, “Get up, and let us fight for our lives, for today is not like yesterday or the day before.
Look, battle is prepared against us in front and behind. The waters of the Jordan surround us on either side, with a thicket in between, and there is no place to turn aside.
Now cry out to the one who dwells in heaven, so that you may be delivered from the hands of your enemies.
They began to fight, and Jonathan raised his hand to strike Bacchides, but Bacchides drew back from him.
Jonathan and those with him turned back and swam across the Jordan, and their enemies did not cross after them.
About a thousand men from Bacchides’ forces fell that day.
Bacchides returned to Jerusalem and built fortified cities in Judea: the fortress at Jericho, Emmaus, Beth-horon, Bethel, Timnath, Pharathon, and Tephon, with high walls, gates, and bars.
He stationed garrisons in them that were hostile to Israel.
He strengthened the city of Beth-zur, Gazara, and the citadel, stationed troops in them, and stored provisions there for them.
Bacchides took the sons of the country's leading men as hostages and placed them under guard in the citadel of Jerusalem.

In the second month of the year 153, Alcimus ordered the wall of the temple's inner courtyard to be demolished. He tore down the work of the prophets and began to carry the destruction through to completion.
At that very time Alcimus was struck down, and his work stopped. He became paralyzed, and his mouth was shut. He could not speak even a single word or give instructions concerning his household.
Alcimus died at that time in great agony.
When Bacchides saw that Alcimus had died, he returned to the king, and the land of Judea had peace and rest for two years.
All the lawless men took counsel together and said, “Look, Jonathan and those with him are living quietly and confidently. Now let us bring Bacchides, and he will capture them all in one night.”
They went and advised him to do this.

Bacchides set out to come with a large army. He secretly sent letters to all his supporters in Judea, telling them to seize Jonathan and everyone with him. But they could not do so, because their plan had been revealed to Jonathan.
Jonathan’s men seized fifty men from among the people of the land who were leaders in this wickedness, and killed them.
Jonathan, Simon, and those with him moved to Beth-jeshan in the wilderness. They rebuilt its ruins and fortified it.
Bacchides learned of this, gathered his whole army, and gave orders to those in Judea.
He marched out and laid siege to Beth-jeshan. He fought against it for many days and constructed siege engines.
Jonathan left his brother Simon inside the city, while he himself went out into the countryside with a contingent of men.
He struck down Adora, his brothers, and the sons of Phasiron in their camp. They began attacking and advancing with their forces.
Simon and those with him came out of the city and burned the siege engines.
They fought against Bacchides, and he was defeated before them. They pressed him hard, because his plan and his expedition had come to nothing.
Bacchides became furiously angry with the lawless men who had advised him to come into the country. He killed many of them and decided to return to his own land.
Jonathan learned of this and sent messengers to him to make peace with him and to have him return their captives.
Bacchides agreed and did as he had requested. He swore to him that he would not seek to harm him for the rest of his life.
He handed over to him the captives he had previously taken from the land of Judea. Then Bacchides returned to his own land and never again entered their territory.
Warfare ceased in Israel. Jonathan settled in Michmash and began to judge the people of Israel and to destroy and eliminate the wicked men from among them.
In the year 160, Alexander, son of Antiochus Epiphanes, son of Antiochus, came up and seized Ptolemais, taking control of it. They welcomed him, and he became king there.
King Demetrius heard about this, gathered a large army, and went out to meet him in battle.
Demetrius sent letters to Jonathan with peaceful words intended to flatter him.
For Demetrius said, “Let us act first and make friendship with him before he goes and makes friendship with Alexander and becomes our enemy.”
For he remembers all the harm we have done to him, his brothers, and his people.”
He gave him authority to gather an army and prepare weapons and to become his ally. He also ordered that the hostages held in the citadel be handed over to him.
Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letters in the hearing of all the people and those living in the citadel.
They were greatly afraid when they heard that the king had given him authority to gather an army.
Those living in the citadel handed the hostages over to Jonathan, and he handed them over to their own people.
Jonathan lived in Jerusalem and began rebuilding and restoring the city.
Jonathan told the workers to build the wall and fortify Mount Zion all around with squared stones. They did so.
The foreigners who were in the fortresses that Bacchides had built fled.
Everyone left his post and went to his own country.
But in Beth-zur some of those who had abandoned the law and the commandments remained, for it had become a place of refuge for them.
King Alexander heard everything that Demetrius had sent and promised to Jonathan, and they told him about the battles, brave deeds, and victories of Jonathan and his brothers.
He said, “Can we find another man like this? Let us now make him our friend and ally.”
He wrote a letter and sent it to him with these words:
“King Alexander to Jonathan, my brother: Greetings.
We have heard about you, that you are a mighty man and are well suited to be our friend.

And now, today we appoint you high priest of your people, so that you may be called the king’s friend. He sent him purple robes and a gold crown and said, “Let him be in agreement with our intentions and maintain friendship with us.”
Jonathan put on the sacred robe in the seventh month of the year 160, at the Festival of Booths. He gathered an army and prepared many weapons.
Demetrius heard these things and was distressed. He said,
“What have we done, that Alexander has acted before us to make friendship with the Jews so that they might become his allies?
I too will write to them with appeals and promises of honor and gifts, so that they may come to our aid.”
He sent them these words: “King Demetrius to the Jewish people: Greetings.
We have heard that you have remained faithful to the covenant with us, maintained your friendship with us, and not joined our enemies, and we are glad.
And now remain loyal to us, and we will repay you with many benefits for what you have done for us.
We will remit many taxes for you and give you great gifts.
And now I exempt you and release all the Jews from tribute, the salt tax, and crown taxes.

From today onward I relinquish the third of the grain and whatever was due to me from the fruit of the trees, so that I will no longer collect it from the land of Judea. From today onward I also remit the three levies imposed on it from Samaria and Galilee.
Jerusalem shall be holy and free, together with all its territory, and I remit the tithes and taxes.
I give the high priest authority over the citadel in Jerusalem, so that he may appoint whomever he wishes to guard it.
Every Jewish person taken captive from the land of Judah anywhere in my kingdom I set free without payment. Everyone is to remit their taxes and the taxes on their livestock.

On all their festivals, Sabbaths, new moons, and appointed days, and for three days before a festival and three days after a festival, all the Jews living in my kingdom shall be exempt and released from taxes.
No one has authority to make demands on any of them or to compel them in any matter whatsoever.
Three thousand Jews shall be enrolled in the king’s forces, and they shall receive allowances appropriate for the king’s forces.

Some of them shall be stationed in the king’s great fortresses, and some shall be appointed to the king’s confidential affairs. Their governors and leaders shall be from among their own people, and they shall be governed according to their own laws, as the king has commanded in the land of Judah.

The three tax districts assigned to Judea from the land of Samaria and from Galilee shall be given to Judea, so that they may all be under one authority, with no one else exercising authority over them except the high priest alone.
I have given Ptolemais and all its territory to the holy people in Jerusalem to meet the expenses of the temple.
I myself will give fifteen thousand pieces of silver every year from the king’s treasury.
Everything owed to me from revenues that have not been paid to me, as with the former nations, shall from now on be given for the work of the temple.
I also relinquish the five thousand pieces of silver that I used to receive every year from the temple’s revenues, because these belong to the priests who serve in the temple.

All who flee and take refuge in the temple in Jerusalem or anywhere within its boundaries, owing a debt to the king or having any other obligation, shall be released, together with everything they possess in my kingdom.
And the temple is to be built and restored.
The wall of Jerusalem shall be rebuilt and strengthened all around, and the expense shall be paid to them from the king’s treasury, also for building the walls of Judea.

But when Jonathan and the people heard these words that Demetrius had sent, they did not believe him or accept his offer, for they remembered all the evil he had done in Israel and how severely he had oppressed them.
Instead, they favored Alexander, because he had been the first to approach them with words of peace, and they supported him continually.
King Alexander gathered a large army and encamped opposite Demetrius.
The two kings began to fight. Demetrius’s army fled, and Alexander pursued them and overpowered them.
The battle grew very fierce and continued until sunset, and Demetrius fell that day.
That day Alexander sent envoys to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, with this message:
Since I have returned to my kingdom, sat on the throne of my ancestors, taken power, defeated Demetrius, grown strong, and taken possession of our lands,
for I fought against him, and he and his army were defeated before us—I have sat on the throne of his kingdom.”
let us now establish friendship with one another. Give me your daughter as my wife, and I will become your son-in-law and give you and her gifts worthy of you.
King Ptolemy answered, “May the day on which you returned to the land of your ancestors and sat on the royal throne be a happy one!
Now I will do everything you have requested in your message. But come to Ptolemais, so that we may meet there, and I will give you my daughter, as you have asked.”
Ptolemy left Egypt with his daughter Cleopatra, and they came to Ptolemais in the year 162.
King Alexander met him, and he gave him his daughter Cleopatra in marriage and celebrated the wedding at Ptolemais with great splendor, as kings do.
King Alexander wrote to Jonathan, asking him to come and meet him.
Jonathan went to Ptolemais with great splendor and met the two kings. He gave them and their friends gold, silver, and gifts, and found favor in their eyes.
Wicked men from Israel, lawless men, gathered before him to bring accusations against Jonathan, but the king paid them no attention and would not listen to them.
The king gave orders, and they took off Jonathan’s clothes and dressed him in purple. When they had done this for him,

The king seated him beside himself and told his officials, “Go out with him into the middle of the city and proclaim that no one is to bring an accusation against him on any matter whatsoever, and no one is to trouble him for any reason whatsoever.”
When those who had been accusing Jonathan saw the honor given him, as heralds proclaimed it before him while he was clothed in purple, they all fled.
The king honored Jonathan, enrolled him among his chief Friends, and appointed him commander of the army and governor of the people.
Jonathan returned to Jerusalem in peace and joy.
In the year 165, Demetrius son of Demetrius came from Crete to the land of his ancestors.
King Alexander heard about it, was deeply distressed, and returned to Antioch.
Demetrius appointed Apollonius, who had been put in charge of Syria. He gathered a large army, camped at Jamnia, and sent a message to Jonathan the high priest, saying:
“You alone are raising yourself up against us, and because of you I have become an object of scorn and ridicule. Why are you exercising authority against us within our territory?
Now, if you trust in your strength, come down to us on the plain, and let us face one another there, for I have an army from the cities with me.
Ask and find out who I am and who our allies are. They say that you cannot stand your ground before us, because your ancestors were defeated twice in their own land.
And now you cannot muster the strength to stand against our army and its cavalry on the plain, where there is neither stone nor crag, nor any place to flee.”
When Jonathan heard the words of Apollonius, he became angry and determined. He chose ten thousand men from Jerusalem, and his brother Simon met him to help him.
Jonathan camped against Joppa, and its inhabitants shut the city gates because Apollonius had a garrison there. They fought against him.
The inhabitants of the city became afraid and opened the gates to them, and Jonathan took control of Joppa.

Apollonius heard about this, took three thousand cavalry and a large army, and went to Azotus as though passing through. He went ahead of them onto the plain because of the cavalry force he had with him, in which he trusted.
Jonathan pursued him to Azotus, and the armies drew together for battle.
Apollonius had left a thousand cavalry behind them in ambush.
Jonathan knew that there was an ambush behind him. They surrounded his camp and shot and let fly their arrows at the troops from morning until evening.
The people stood firm, as Jonathan had commanded, and their enemies’ cavalry grew weary.
Simon brought up his army and fought against the divisions until the cavalry and the troops broke ranks, were defeated, and fled before him.
The cavalry scattered across the plain and fled to Azotus. They entered the temple of Dagon, their idol, to save themselves.
Jonathan burned the temple of their idol, and those who had fled for refuge into the temple of Dagon he burned along with it. He also burned Azotus and the towns around it and took their plunder.
Those who fell by the sword, together with those who were burned, numbered about eight thousand men.
Jonathan moved on from there and camped at Ashkelon. The inhabitants of the city came out to meet him with great honor.
Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his companions, bringing a great deal of plunder with them.
When King Alexander heard these things, he praised Jonathan still more.
He sent him a gold clasp, such as is customarily given to members of royal families, and gave him Ekron and all its territory as a hereditary possession.
The king of Egypt gathered a great army, like the sand on the seashore, and many ships. He intended to seize Alexander’s kingdom by deceit and add it to his own kingdom.
He set out for Syria with peaceful words. The inhabitants of the cities opened their gates to him and welcomed him, because Alexander had ordered them to welcome him as his father-in-law.
As Ptolemy entered the cities, he left troops and guards in each of them.

When he reached Azotus, they showed him the temple of the idol Dagon, burned down, and Azotus and all its surrounding towns in ruins. They showed him the bodies lying there and the burned remains of those he had burned in the battle, which they had piled in heaps along the road.
They told the king everything he had done, intending to discredit him. But when the king heard it, he remained silent.
Jonathan met the king at Joppa with great praise. They greeted one another and spent the night there.
Jonathan accompanied the king as far as the river called Eleutherus, and then returned to Jerusalem.
King Ptolemy took control of all the cities along the coast as far as Seleucia by the sea, and he plotted evil against Alexander.
He sent messengers to King Demetrius, saying, “Come, let us make a treaty with one another. I will give you my daughter, whom Alexander married, and you will reign over your father’s kingdom.”
For I regret giving him my daughter, because he wanted to kill me.”
He despised and rejected him because he coveted his kingdom.
