He took his daughter away from him and gave her to Demetrius. He turned against Alexander, and his hostility became openly known.
Ptolemy entered Antioch and put on the crown of Asia. He placed two crowns on his head, those of Asia and Egypt.
King Alexander was in Cilicia at that time, because the people of that region had rebelled against him.
Alexander heard about this and came against him in battle. Ptolemy went out to meet him with a large army and a strong force, and defeated Alexander.
Alexander fled to Arabia to hide there, while King Ptolemy rose to power.
Zabdiel the Arab took Alexander's head and sent it to Ptolemy.
King Ptolemy himself also died three days later, and those he had left in the fortresses were killed there by the people of those places.
Demetrius became king in the year one hundred and sixty-seven.
In those days Jonathan gathered an army from Judea to fight against those occupying the citadel in Jerusalem, and he made many siege engines against it.
Some men who were hated by their people, wicked men, went to the king and told him, “Jonathan is now besieging the citadel.”

When the king heard this, he became angry. As soon as he heard it, he set out and came to Ptolemais. He wrote to Jonathan, telling him not to continue besieging the citadel, but to come and meet him quickly in Ptolemais.
When Jonathan heard this, however, he ordered them to continue besieging the citadel. He chose some of the priests and elders of Israel and put his own life at risk.
He took gold, silver, vessels, and various other gifts and went to the king at Ptolemais, and he found favor with him.
Wicked men from among the people were bringing accusations against him.
The king treated him as his predecessor had treated him and honored him before all his friends.
The king granted him the priesthood and all the honor he had previously held. He promoted him and made him one of his great and honored friends.
Jonathan persuaded the king to exempt Judea from paying tribute, along with the three districts of the region and Samaria, and promised him three hundred talents.
The king agreed and wrote Jonathan letters concerning everything he had requested. They read as follows:
“King Demetrius to Jonathan, my brother, and to the Jewish people: Greetings.
Copy of the letter: “We have written to Lasthenes our kinsman about you, and we are also writing to you so that you too may know.
‘King Demetrius to Lasthenes, my father: Greetings.
“We wish to show kindness to the Jewish people, our friends who keep peace with us, because of their goodwill toward us.

“We have confirmed and granted to them the territory of Judea and the three districts of Ephraim, Lydda, and Ramathaim, which were added to Judea from Samaria, together with all their dependencies, for the offerings in Jerusalem, in place of the royal taxes formerly collected from them on the crops of the land and the fruit of the trees.
“As for the other payments that were due to us from tithes, customs duties, salt pools, and crown levies, all are remitted to them.
Not one of these provisions is to be revoked from now on.
“Now take care to make a copy of these decrees and give it to Jonathan, and let it be displayed in a prominent and public place on the holy mountain.”

King Demetrius saw that the land was quiet and at peace under his rule and that no one opposed him. He dismissed his entire army, each man to his own home, except for those he had recruited from the islands of the nations. Then all the troops who had served his ancestors became hostile to him.

Now Trypho had formerly belonged to Alexander’s household. He saw that the entire army was grumbling against Demetrius, and he went to Malchus the Arab, who was bringing up Antiochus, Alexander’s son.

He asked him to hand the boy over to him so that he could make him king in his father’s place. He told him everything Demetrius had done and about the hostility his army had shown him, and he stayed there for many days.
Jonathan sent word to King Demetrius, asking him to remove those occupying the citadel from Jerusalem, as well as those occupying the fortresses, for they were fighting against Israel.
Demetrius sent word to Jonathan, saying, “I will not only do these things for you and your people, but I will also bestow great honor on you and your people when I have the opportunity.
“But now you would do well to send me men to help me, for my entire army has deserted me.”
Jonathan sent three thousand valiant men to Antioch. They came to the king, and the king was delighted at their arrival.
All the inhabitants of the city, about one hundred and twenty thousand, gathered in the center of the city, intending to kill King Demetrius.
The king fled into the palace, and the townspeople seized all the exits from the city and began fighting.
The king called on the Jews to help him. They all gathered around him together, then spread throughout the city, and that day they killed about one hundred thousand people in the city.
They burned the city, took a great deal of plunder that day, and rescued the king.
The inhabitants of the city saw that the Jews had gained the upper hand and had taken control of the entire city as they wished. They lost heart and cried out to the king in supplication, saying:
“Give us your pledge, and let the Jews stop fighting against us and the city.”
They threw down their weapons, pledged peace, and made peace. The Jews were greatly honored before the king and throughout his kingdom, and they returned to Jerusalem with a great deal of plunder.
King Demetrius sat on his royal throne, and the land became quiet and peaceful under him.
He proved false in everything he had said, turned against Jonathan, and did not give him everything he had promised him. He put Jonathan under great pressure.
After this, Tryphon returned with the young boy Antiochus, who became king and put on the crown.
All the troops that Demetrius had dispersed gathered around him. He fought against Demetrius, and Demetrius was defeated and fled.
Tryphon took all his animals and captured Antioch.
The young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan, saying, “I confirm you in the high priesthood, give you authority over all four districts, and appoint you as one of the king’s Friends.”
He sent him gold vessels and a table service, and gave him permission to drink from gold vessels and wear purple garments with a gold clasp on them.
He appointed his brother Simon governor from the borders of Tyre to the border of Egypt.

Jonathan set out and traveled through the regions beyond the river and through the cities. The entire Syrian army gathered around him to support him. Jonathan came to Ashkelon, and the inhabitants of the city welcomed him with great acclaim.
From there he went to Gaza, but the people of Gaza shut their gates against him. He besieged it, burned all its surrounding area, and plundered it.

The people of Gaza appealed to Jonathan, and he pledged peace to them. He took the sons of their leading men as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem. Then he traveled through the country as far as Damascus.
Jonathan heard that Demetrius’s commanders had come to Kedesh in Galilee with a large army, intending to put an end to his activities.
He went to meet them, but left his brother Simon in the country.
Simon besieged Beth-zur and fought against it for many days, keeping its inhabitants shut in.
They asked him to pledge peace to them, and he did so. He brought them out of there, took possession of the city, and stationed a garrison in it.
Jonathan and his army camped by the waters of Gennesaret. Early in the morning they went to the plain of Hazor.
There the army of the Philistines met him on the plain, and they sent men to lie in ambush against him.
The men rose from behind them and began to fight, and all Jonathan’s men fled.
None of them remained with him except Mattathias son of Absalom, Judas son of Chalphi, and the chief military officers.
Jonathan tore his clothes, put dust on his head, and prayed.
He turned against them in battle and defeated them, and they fled.
When those who had been with him saw the enemy fleeing, they turned back and joined him. They pursued them as far as Qalas [?], their camp, and camped there.
About three thousand Philistine men fell that day, and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.
Jonathan saw that circumstances favored him, so he chose men and sent them to Rome to confirm and renew their friendship with the Romans.
He also sent letters to the Spartans and to other places in the same way.
They went to Rome, entered the senate house, and said to them, “Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish people have sent us to renew the friendship and alliance as before.”
The Romans welcomed them gladly and gave them letters directing that, in every region they passed through, they should be sent safely on their way to the land of Judah.
This is a copy of the letter Jonathan sent to the Spartans:
Jonathan the high priest, the elders, the priests, and all the Jewish people, to our brothers the Spartans: greetings.
For even now letters have been sent to Onias the high priest from Darius your king, stating that you are our brothers, as the letters show.
Onias had received the man who was sent with honor, and had accepted these letters, which spoke of alliance and friendship.
We, however, do not rely on these things, because we have the holy books in our hands to comfort us.
Nevertheless, we wished to send to you to renew our friendship and brotherhood with you, so that we might not become strangers to you. For a long time has passed since you sent word to us.
We always remember you without fail at the festivals and on the appointed days, in every sacrifice we offer and in all our prayers, as it is necessary and right to remember one’s brothers.
We rejoice greatly in your glory.
Many troubles have surrounded us, and all the kings around us have waged great wars against us.
We did not wish to trouble you or the rest of our friends and allies in all our wars.
For we have help from heaven, which supports us, has rescued us from our enemies, and has humbled them before us.
We chose Numenius [?] son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason and sent them to the Romans to renew our alliance and friendship with them.
We instructed them to come to you as well, greet you, and give you our letters concerning the renewal of our brotherhood with you.
Now you will do well to write us copies of these things.”
This is a copy of the letter he had sent:
“Aniris, king of the Spartans, to Onias the great high priest: Greetings.
It has been found in a written document concerning the Spartans and the Jews that they are brothers and are descended from Abraham.
Now that we have learned these things, you will do well to write to us about your welfare.
We are writing to you about everything concerning us, because everything you have is ours, and everything we have is yours. We have instructed them to tell you all these things.
Jonathan heard that the commanders of Demetrius’s forces had returned with an army much larger than the first to fight against him.
Jonathan set out from Jerusalem and met them in the land of Hamath, for he would not give them an opportunity to invade his land.
He sent spies to their camp. They returned and told him, “They are planning to attack you during the night.”
When the sun had set, Jonathan ordered those with him to stay awake, keep their weapons ready, and remain prepared for battle throughout the night. He posted guards outside the camp, all around it.
Their enemies heard that Jonathan and those with him were prepared for battle. They were afraid and trembled in their hearts, and they left fires burning in their camps and fled.
But Jonathan and those with him did not know until morning, for they could see the fires burning.
Jonathan pursued them but did not catch them, for they had crossed the river called Eleutherus.
Jonathan turned against the Arabs called the Zabadeans, defeated them, and took their plunder.
He set out and came to Damascus, passing through the territories.
Simon went out and traveled as far as Ashkelon and the fortresses around it. Then he turned toward Joppa and captured it.
For he heard that they wanted to hand the fortress over to Demetrius’s men, so he stationed a garrison there to guard it.
Jonathan returned, gathered the elders of the people, and consulted with them about building fortresses in Judea

And let us raise the walls of Jerusalem. They built a high barrier between the citadel and the city, separating it from the city, so that the city would be independent of it and they could neither buy nor sell.
They gathered to rebuild the city. A section of the wall beside the valley on the east collapsed and buried the place called Chaphenatha.
Simon built up Adida in the plain and strengthened it with gates and bars.
Trypho wanted to become king over Asia, put on the crown, and lay hands on King Antiochus.
He was afraid that Jonathan would not leave him alone, or might fight against him. He was looking for an opportunity to seize Jonathan and destroy him, so he set out and came to Beth-shan.
Jonathan went out with forty thousand men chosen for battle and came to Beth-shan.
Trypho saw that Jonathan had come with a large army, and he was afraid to lay hands on him.

He welcomed him with praise and honored him before all his friends. He gave him gifts and told his friends to do the same, and they too gave gifts to him and his army. He ordered them to obey Jonathan as they obeyed him.
He said to Jonathan, “Why have you gone to the trouble of bringing all these people when we are not at war?

“Now send them away, each to his own home, and choose a few men to stay with you. Come with me to Ptolemais, and I will hand it over to you, along with the other fortresses, the remaining troops, and all those in charge of affairs. Then I will turn back and leave, for that is why I came.”
Jonathan believed him and did as he said. He sent his army away, and it went to the land of Judea.
He kept three thousand men with him. He left two thousand of them in Galilee, while one thousand went with him.
When Jonathan entered the city of Ptolemais, they imprisoned him there and killed with the sword everyone who had entered with him.
Trypho sent troops and cavalry to Galilee and the Great Plain to destroy all of Jonathan’s men.
They learned that Jonathan had been captured and that he and those with him had perished. They took courage, encouraged one another, and marched together in battle formation.
Their pursuers saw that they were embittered to the point of death and were fighting with all their strength, so they turned back from pursuing them.
They all reached the land of Judah safely. They mourned for Jonathan and those with him and were filled with great fear. All Israel mourned deeply.

All the nations around them wanted to destroy them completely, for they said, “They have no leader or anyone to help them. Now come, let us fight against them and erase their memory from among humankind.”
Simon heard that Trypho had gathered a large army to invade the land of Judea and devastate it.
He saw that the people were afraid and trembling, and he went up to Jerusalem.

He gathered the people, encouraged them, and said to them, “You know everything that I, my brothers, and my father’s whole household have done for the law and the sanctuary, and the battles and hardships we have endured.
For this reason all my brothers died for the sake of all Israel, and I alone am left.
Now, far be it from me to spare myself in any time of distress, for I am no better than my brothers.
But I will fight for my people, for our sanctuary, and for our children, because all the nations have gathered to destroy us out of their hatred.”
The spirit of the people was stirred and fired up as soon as they heard his words.
They answered him loudly, “You are our leader in place of your brothers Judas and Jonathan.
Fight our battles, and we will do everything you tell us.”
Simon gathered all the fighting men and hurried to finish and complete the wall of Jerusalem. He strengthened it all the way around.
He sent Jonathan son of Absalom to Joppa with a large army. Jonathan drove out those who were in it and settled there himself.
Trypho set out from Ptolemais with a large army to enter the land of Judah. Jonathan was with him under guard.
Simon camped at Adida, facing the plain.
Trypho learned that Simon had taken the place of his brother Jonathan and was ready to fight against him. He sent messengers to him, saying,
“We are holding your brother Jonathan because of money he owed the royal treasury in connection with the responsibilities he held.
Now send one hundred talents of silver and two of his sons as hostages, so that when we release him he will not turn against us and break away from us. Then we will release him.”
Simon knew that they were speaking deceitfully to him, but he sent the money and the boys, lest he provoke great hostility against Israel.
because he had not sent the money and the boys, and so they had perished.
He sent the boys and a hundred talents, but Tryphon lied and did not release Jonathan.
After this, Tryphon came to march through the land of Judah and lay it waste. He went by the road to Adora, but Simon and his army confronted him wherever he went.
The inhabitants of the citadel sent messengers to Tryphon, asking him to come to them quickly through the wilderness and send them provisions.
Tryphon prepared all his cavalry to come that night, but there was heavy snow, and he could not come because of the snow. So he set out and went to Gilead.
When Tryphon reached Baskama, he killed Jonathan, and Jonathan was buried there.
Then Tryphon turned back and went to his own land.
Simon sent for the bones of his brother Jonathan and buried him at Modein, in the city of his ancestors.
All Israel wept and mourned for him for many days.
Simon built a monument over the tomb of his father and his brothers, raising it high so that it could be seen, with dressed stones carved on both sides.
He erected seven monuments, facing one another, for his father, his mother, and his four brothers.

He made structures and set up great columns for them. On the columns he carved every kind of weapon of war as an everlasting memorial. Beside the weapons he made carved ships and raised them high so that everyone who sailed the sea could see them.
The tomb that Simon built in Modin [?] is there to this day.
Meanwhile, Trypho dealt treacherously with Antiochus, the great king, and killed him.
He became king in his place, put on the crown of Asia, and brought great suffering upon the land.
Simon rebuilt the fortresses of Judah and surrounded them with high towers, great walls, gates, and bars. He stored provisions in the fortresses.
Simon chose men and sent them to King Demetrius to obtain relief for the land, because all Tryphon's actions had been acts of plunder.
King Demetrius sent him a reply in a letter with these words:
“King Demetrius to Simon, the high priest and friend of the king, and to the elders and the Jewish people: Greetings.
We have received the gold crown and the delegation you sent us. We are ready to establish a lasting peace with you and to write to the officials in charge of affairs to exempt you from taxes.
Everything we have written to you remains in force, and the fortresses you have built shall belong to you.
We also pardon the sins and offenses committed up to this day and remit the crown tribute you owed. From now on, no one who paid tax in Jerusalem is to pay it.
Any of your people who wish to enroll among our men may enroll, and let there be peace between us.”
In the year 170, the yoke of the nations was lifted from Israel.
The people began to write documents and conduct transactions with the wording, “In the first year, in the name of Simon, the great high priest, ruler, and leader of the Jews.”
In those days Simon laid siege to Gaza and surrounded it with his army. He made strong wooden towers and brought them up to the city wall. He battered down one tower and captured the city.
The soldiers leaped out of the wooden towers and descended into the city, and there was great turmoil within the city.
The inhabitants of the city came up with their wives and children, tearing their clothes and crying out loudly. They asked Simon to give them a pledge of peace.
They said to him, “Do not treat us according to our wickedness, but according to your kindness.”
Simon spared them and did not fight them, but expelled them from the city. He purified the houses where there had been idols, and then entered the city, offering praise and blessing.
He removed all impurity from it and settled there men who delighted in the Law. He built a fortress in it and made a house for himself there.
The inhabitants of the citadel in Jerusalem were prevented from going in or out, buying or selling. They suffered severe hunger, and many of them died of starvation.
They asked Simon to give them a pledge of peace, and he gave it to them. He brought them out of there and purified the citadel of all its impurity.

They entered the citadel on the twenty-third day of the second month in the year 171, with rejoicing, songs of praise, shouts of hosanna, lyres, and harps, because a great enemy had been crushed and removed from Israel, and the foreigner had ceased fighting against Israel.
They decreed that this day should be celebrated every year with festivity and rejoicing.
They fortified the Temple hill beside the citadel, and Simon lived there with his household.
Simon saw that his son John was a valiant man and appointed him commander of all the forces. John lived in Gezer.
In the year 172, Demetrius gathered his army and went to Media to gather forces for himself and fight against Tryphon.
Arsaces, king of Persia and Media, heard that Demetrius had entered his territory, and he sent one of his commanders to capture him alive.
He went and attacked Demetrius’s army, captured him, brought him to Arsaces, and put him in prison.
The land was quiet and at rest throughout Simon's days. He did good things for his people, and they were pleased with his rule and his glory throughout his days.
Along with all his glory, he took Joppa as a harbor and made an entrance for ships of the sea.
He widened and extended his people’s borders and gained possession of all their land.
He gathered many captives and gained control of Gezer, Beth-zur, and the citadel. He swept away and removed all impurity from them, and no one opposed him.
They lived in peace and cultivated their land, and the earth yielded its crops and the trees of the land their fruit.
The elders sat in the public squares, and all of them deliberated about good things. The young men clothed themselves in glory, not in weapons of war.
He supplied the cities with provisions and strengthened them with defensive equipment, until his glorious name became known to all the ends of the earth.
He established peace in the land, and Israel enjoyed great prosperity.
Everyone sat beneath their own vines and fig trees, and there was no one to disturb them.
Their enemies were completely destroyed and removed from among them, and the warriors from the land. Even kings were crushed in those days.
He supported and strengthened all the poor of his people. He wiped out and removed all wickedness, injustice, and evil, and commanded obedience to the law.
He adorned the sanctuary and increased the number of vessels in the temple.
The Romans heard that Jonathan had died, and the Spartans also heard, and they were deeply distressed.
But when they heard that his brother Simon had become high priest in his place and controlled the land, the cities, and everything in them,
they wrote to him on a bronze tablet to renew with him the friendship and alliance that they had established with his brothers Judas and Jonathan.
It was read before the assembly in Jerusalem.

This is the copy of the letter that the Spartans sent: “The rulers of the Spartans and the cities, to Simon the great high priest, to the elders and priests, and to the rest of the Jewish people, our brothers: Greetings.
The elders who were sent to us told us about your peace, your honor, and your glory, and we were very glad at their arrival.
We recorded everything they said in our people's council chamber, as follows: ‘Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, elders of the Jews, came to us to renew their friendship with us.’

The people were pleased to accept their friendship. They received the men with honor and deposited a copy of their letters in the archives, so that they would remain as a memorial for the Spartan people. They also sent Simon the high priest copies of these letters and the replies to them.
After this, Simon sent Numenius to Rome, carrying a large gold shield weighing a thousand minas, to establish an alliance with them.
When the people heard these things, they said, “What kindness can we give in return to Simon the high priest and his sons?”
